analysis.one_liner: Sets national ballast water and import screening standards to keep invasive species out of U.S. waters.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to curb ship-borne invasive species, with 77 cosponsors, died in House committees without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required all ships in U.S. waters to manage and treat their ballast water — the water ships carry for stability that spreads organisms from port to port — under enforceable national standards with civil and criminal penalties. It also would have screened newly imported live aquatic species, funded early detection and rapid-response programs, and completed an electric barrier on the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal to keep invasive fish out of the Great Lakes. The bill was referred to two House committees and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal and Great Lakes communities, commercial and recreational fisheries, water utilities, and boaters. Invasive species already cost the economy billions of dollars a year — about $3 billion was spent in a decade fighting the zebra mussel alone — and the bill's approach was to stop new introductions, which it called the cheapest and most effective strategy.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fisheries, Great Lakes towns, water utilities

how_it_helps.text: Requires every ballast-equipped vessel in U.S. waters to carry an invasive species management plan and meet mandatory ballast water exchange or treatment standards, with civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation and criminal penalties for knowing violations.
Prohibits importing live aquatic organisms of species not already in trade unless they pass a federal risk screening, closing a pathway that currently operates with little oversight.

Creates a national early detection and monitoring system, approves and funds state rapid-response plans with a federal cost share of at least 50 percent, and establishes federal rapid response teams in all ten federal regions.

Directs completion and operation of the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal dispersal barrier to block invasive species such as Asian carp from moving between the Great Lakes and Mississippi River basins.

analysis.who_pays: Ocean shipping companies, which would have to install ballast treatment systems or perform at-sea exchanges, redesign new vessels built after 2006, and keep inspection records. Importers in the aquarium, pet, aquaculture, and horticulture trades would face screening and possible bans on new species, with fees agencies could raise to cover screening costs.

drawbacks.text: Ballast water exchange on the high seas can genuinely endanger a vessel in bad weather; the bill handles this with a safety exemption letting each ship's master skip the exchange, but that exemption also creates a gap in protection, and compliance relies on the master's good-faith judgment.

Treatment equipment, new-vessel design requirements, and screening fees would raise costs for shipping lines and the aquarium and aquaculture trades, costs that could be passed on in freight rates and the price of ornamental fish and farmed seafood.

The interim standard — killing or removing at least 95 percent of live organisms in ballast discharge — still allows some organisms through, and final standards were not required until four years after enactment, so protection would have ramped up slowly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's own findings put invasive species costs at billions of dollars per year, including roughly $3 billion spent over ten years on a single invader, the zebra mussel. Against that, the compliance costs to shipping and importers look modest, and prevention is the cheapest form of control. The main honest objections are the safety risk of mandatory at-sea exchanges in rough weather and the slow timetable for final standards. On balance, a well-designed preventive bill whose benefits to fisheries, water infrastructure, and ecosystems likely exceeded its industry costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees and their subcommittees until the Congress ended in January 2007, and never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Introduced April 13, 2005 by Rep. Wayne Gilchrest with four original cosponsors from both parties, the bill drew 77 cosponsors in total: 53 Democrats, 23 Republicans, and 1 Independent.
The Speaker referred it to both the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Resources Committee, splitting jurisdiction over its provisions.

Within days it was sent to the Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment and the Resources Subcommittee on Fisheries and Oceans, and no further action of any kind was taken.
No committee reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled in either chamber, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ocean shipping companies and importers of live aquatic organisms were better off, since they avoided new ballast treatment and screening requirements. State and federal agencies also avoided new program costs, while the public continued to bear the billions of dollars in annual damage from invasive species.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was strongly bipartisan — 53 Democrats, 23 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but because no vote was ever held, the record shows no roll-call split; the committees that let the bill die were run by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would have required ballast water management plans, mandatory exchange or treatment standards, and inspection records for every ballast-equipped vessel, with penalties up to $50,000 per violation. Ships' ballast discharge is the main pathway for invasive species, so the industry's cost avoidance came at the public's expense in continued ecological and infrastructure damage.

industries.industry: Aquarium, pet, and live aquatic organism import trade
industries.note: New species not already in trade could not be imported without federal screening and approval, with possible prohibition and fees to cover screening costs. The trade's interest in unrestricted imports ran against the public's interest in keeping invasive species out.

Mandatory treatment standards for existing and newly built vessels would have created a large market for treatment systems, with federal approval processes and technical assistance for shipowners installing them.

Imported species cultured in the U.S. would face screening by the Secretary of Agriculture, adding compliance costs, but the bill also included education and outreach programs promoting voluntary cooperation with the aquaculture industry.
